Header:
Date: 2026-04-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~48min | Attendees: Jamie Chen, Ravi Patel (Redwood) - Maria Gonzales, Evan Lee, Priya Desai (Sentinel)

[00:00:00] Jamie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jamie, AE at Redwood - Ravi our solutions engineer is here too. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:10] Maria: Good, thanks. We wanted a practical walkthrough of the SDKs - python/ts - and a sense for auth and setup. We've skimmed the docs.
[00:00:18] Jamie: Perfect. We'll do a quick run through the Python quickstart, then TypeScript, cover auth patterns (API key, SSO, KMS), env setup, and then show Console + Optimize suggestions.
[00:00:30] Ravi: I'll share my screen, starting with the repo quickstart. Bear with me, screen is up.
[00:00:45] Ravi: Ok, so repo layout - we have a simple example: requirements.txt, sdk client usage in main.py. Key point: install redwood-inference SDK via pip, or npm package @redwood/inference for TS. Example command: pip install redwood-inference==0.9.2 (note: minor versions vary).
[00:01:20] Evan: Quick question - do you have separate packages for streaming and embeddings or is it unified?
[00:01:30] Ravi: It's unified; same client exposes streaming, chat, embeddings. The streaming API is via stream() or async iterators in Python, and event emitter pattern in TypeScript.
[00:01:45] Ravi: Example Python snippet:
    from redwood import Client
    client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
    resp = client.chat.create(model='redwood-2-small', messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize..."}])

[00:02:10] Maria: Okay - auth wise we plan to use short lived API keys and vault them. How do you recommend KMS integration?
[00:02:20] Jamie: For Hosted API most customers use API keys rotated and stored in your secret manager (Hashi, AWS Secrets Manager). For Private/Dedicated you can integrate Redwood with your KMS/HSM so keys never leave your control. We have docs on KMS binding - I'll share the whitepaper.
[00:02:40] Priya: Do you support SSO for console access and fine-grained RBAC?
[00:02:46] Jamie: Yes, Console supports SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning. RBAC is per-project with roles for deploy, read, billing. For API keys you can scope them to routes/usage.
[00:02:59] Evan: How do you recommend environment separation - dev vs staging - is it env vars and different API keys?
[00:03:05] Ravi: Exactly. We recommend using separate projects in Console per environment or separate API keys with policies. Example: REDWOOD_API_KEY_DEV, REDWOOD_API_KEY_STAGING. For Dedicated you can have isolated pools for staging.
[00:03:20] Jamie: We'll send a sample layout for repo + CI, including GitHub Actions snippet to fetch secrets and run smoke tests against staging.
[00:03:30] Maria: Great. Can you demo a live request and then show the Console side?
[00:03:35] Ravi: Yup. Running main.py now - minor lag because my network is choppy.
[00:03:55] Speaker 1: (background) and you'll see the streaming tokens come in, there might be a small jitter on my end.
[00:04:05] Ravi: Response streamed, we handle partials, client.on('token') in TS or async for in Python to consume. Also show error handling - rate limit (429) with Retry-After header and exponential backoff sample.
[00:04:25] Evan: For throughput do you recommend batching? We have a bunch of small requests per user event.
[00:04:30] Ravi: Yes batching and caching is key. Redwood Optimize suggests batching thresholds per route; it gives estimated cost savings and latency impact. We'll demonstrate Optimize recommendations in the Console in a bit.
[00:04:45] Jamie: On deployment options - you mentioned compliance requirements - Sentinel is in payments space, yes?
[00:04:51] Maria: Correct. SOC2 and data residency are musts. We may prefer Private deployment if we need on-prem or VPC with customer-managed KMS.
[00:04:59] Jamie: Understood - Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem with audit logs and encryption at rest. We'll attach the SOC2 report and a checklist.
[00:05:12] Priya: How are logs handled? We need redactable logs and audit trails.
[00:05:17] Ravi: Audit logs include user actions in Console; request/response logs can be configured to exclude PII or to send to your SIEM. We support forwarders (CloudWatch, Splunk). There's also optional request scrubbing.
[00:05:33] Maria: Good. Now TypeScript quickstart?
[00:05:36] Ravi: Switching to TS - npm install @redwood/inference. Example:
    import Redwood from '@redwood/inference';
    const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
    const res = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-2', prompt: '...' });

[00:06:05] Evan: Any gotchas with bundlers and keys?
[00:06:08] Ravi: Don't bundle secrets into front-end bundles; call from server-side or use proxy endpoints. For client-side use cases we provide edge-safe tokens and short lived keys via token exchange patterns.
[00:06:22] Maria: Can we do function/tool calling from the SDK?
[00:06:26] Ravi: Yes, you can define tools and pass a tool schema. Tool calling works in both Python and TS. It's similar to the open model patterns; our SDK helpers make it simpler.
[00:06:38] Speaker 2: There's an example tool for fetching customer profile in the repo.
[00:06:44] Jamie: Quick note on model catalog - we'll recommend model variants for latency/cost. For high throughput we can point you at smaller float16/quantized variants.
[00:06:56] Evan: How do upgrades/rollouts work? We want to pin a model version and then roll forward.
[00:07:00] Ravi: Console supports model pinning and rollout policies: canary percentages, automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if SLOs breach. We also expose per-route metrics so you can A/B test.
[00:07:12] Maria: Could you show Optimize suggestions for one of our sample routes?
[00:07:16] Ravi: I'll pull up Console - bear with small delay.
[00:07:35] Ravi: In Console > Routes you can see token breakdown, cost per 1k tokens, and suggestions. For example the Optimize panel recommended prefix caching for our lookup route and lowering max tokens to 256 which would save ~32% on cost.
[00:07:55] Priya: Is there an automated eval to catch regressions? We need to ensure quality doesn't degrade.
[00:08:00] Jamie: Yes, Redwood has evals tied to prompt sets; you can configure regression alerts on a test set. We'll share the eval playbook.
[00:08:10] Evan: Back to SDK - what about local dev offline mode? Can we run a small local server or mock?
[00:08:16] Ravi: We provide a dev proxy that can replay recorded responses or stub responses. It's not a full model runtime locally. For self-hosted Private you can run inference in your infra.
[00:08:30] Maria: About billing and quotas - we need predictable spend.
[00:08:34] Jamie: For Hosted we provide usage-based billing and quotas; for Dedicated there's reserved capacity contracts and predictable throughput. We'll include a pricing matrix in the follow-up.
[00:08:46] Evan: Any latency numbers you can share for the model variants?
[00:08:50] Ravi: We have perf profiles by model and region - for example redwood-2-small ~80ms p50 on T4, redwood-2-medium ~150ms. These are illustrative; we'll share our benchmark sheet.
[00:09:06] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) sometimes the names in the docs get garbled, e.g., KV cache spelled K-V cache, little OCR-ish errors in the auto notes.
[00:09:18] Jamie: Ha, yeah auto transcripts do that.
[00:09:25] Ravi: Quick demo of error handling pattern in TS: try/catch around client.generate, check resp.status, on 503 fallback to cached answer or alternate model route.
[00:09:40] Maria: For pilot we're thinking 2-week POC with 100k tokens/day baseline and then scale. Are there capacity constraints we should know?
[00:09:48] Ravi: For pilot hosted is fine; if you need strict isolation or predictable latency we recommend Dedicated. We can reserve a burst pool for the pilot.
[00:09:59] Priya: Security review - Can we schedule a deeper call with your security team?
[00:10:03] Jamie: Absolutely - I'll loop in our security PM. We can do a 60-min security review covering SOC2, encryption, and network design.
[00:10:12] Maria: Great.
[00:10:20] Speaker 3: (short silence)
[00:13:00] Ravi: (jump ahead) Now show CI snippet: GH Actions job that uses REDWOOD_API_KEY_STAGING secret, runs smoke tests, posts to Slack. Example YAML at docs.redwood.ai/ci-samples.
[00:15:30] Evan: About SDK versions - how stable is the TS API?
[00:15:35] Jamie: Semver, we maintain compatibility guarantees; major versions only on breaking changes and we provide migration guides.
[00:18:10] Maria: Any gotchas integrating with our Java services? We can call Node microservices or Python.
[00:18:16] Ravi: Use a small proxy service to centralize calls and secrets - recommended for polyglot environments.
[00:20:00] Jamie: Ok recap - we'll send the following: pricing/DED vs hosted, SOC2 + security pack, benchmark sheet, sample CI/quickstart repos, and a proposed pilot plan.
[00:20:20] Maria: Yes that's what we need. Timeline - we aim to decide by end of month.
[00:20:25] Jamie: Sounds good. We'll aim to have proposal and attachments by Friday.
[00:20:35] Priya: Please include details about data retention and log forwarding.
[00:20:40] Jamie: Will do.
[00:20:50] Ravi: Any final technical questions?
[00:21:00] Evan: One last - streaming partials and token-level costs - can we get per-token costs broken down?
[00:21:05] Ravi: Console gives token-level breakdown and per-route cost. Optimize can estimate savings per suggestion.
[00:21:20] Maria: ok thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[00:21:30] Jamie: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up with the docs and proposal.
